claims.text: FeCoNiCrAl feedstock with a particle-size range of 15–45 μm currently produces an HVOF coating of insufficient thickness.
Reducing stand-off distance while increasing particle temperature and velocity will produce a thicker FeCoNiCrAl coating than standard HVOF parameters.
The proposed parameter changes will preserve coating integrity.
The proposed parameter changes will limit as-sprayed oxidation.
Increasing particle temperature enhances particle melting.
Increasing particle velocity raises particle kinetic energy at impact.
Enhanced melting and impact kinetic energy improve splat flattening and inter-splat bonding.
Improved splat flattening and inter-splat bonding produce a thicker, denser coating.
Reducing stand-off distance shortens the particles' high-temperature flight time.
Shorter high-temperature flight time reduces oxygen exposure and unwanted in-flight oxidation.
Higher particle temperature and velocity improve deposition efficiency and splat deformation, thereby increasing coating build-up.
The modified process will yield a bond-coat thickness significantly exceeding 45 μm.
The modified coating will retain microstructural integrity and have lower as-sprayed oxidation than coatings made with conventional parameters.

The intervention remains effective under standard bond-coat spraying conditions with controlled oxygen partial pressure and substrate temperatures typical of high-temperature aerospace or turbine service.
Excessively high particle temperatures or excessively short stand-off distances may reduce adhesion or increase oxidation.
The proposed experiment compares optimized and standard HVOF processing on identical substrates while holding feedstock, substrate preparation, and atmosphere constant.
Failure to increase coating thickness significantly, or a significant oxidation increase that compromises integrity or exceeds a preset threshold, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 15–45 μm value is introduced as the feedstock particle-size range, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule treat it as the baseline coating-thickness range. Feedstock size and deposited coating thickness are different quantities.

The intervention invokes increased particle temperature as part of the route to low oxidation, whereas the boundary acknowledges that sufficiently high temperature can increase oxidation. No quantitative operating window resolves this tension.
